overview: Candidates attempted most MCQs, used the jotting space well and handled powers of ten on calculators competently.
Solutions were generally well structured with clear rearrangement, substitution and appropriate significant figures.
Avoid rounding in the middle of multi-step calculations; premature rounding still cost marks.
Use correct technical terms (photon, work function, frequency) rather than bare symbols in written explanations, or define every symbol used.
Use the Data, Formulae and Relationships booklet for constants such as e and the electron mass.
Newton's third law, conditions for equilibrium and the vector nature of momentum were notable weaknesses; Questions 5, 9 and 13 were hardest in Section A.
assessment_for_learning: Annotate MCQ diagrams and text and write down the key equation; minimal relevant jottings often lead straight to the answer.
Read every statement in a question carefully - skimming one pivotal condition (e.g. constant volume) leads to a plausible but wrong answer.
When a diagram supports an answer, label it fully (normals, angles measured from the normal).
Write word equations such as photon energy = work function + maximum KE instead of just quoting hf = phi + KEmax.
Be concise; an additional answer space is available but should only be used when needed.

1.mcq_distractor: D was the most popular distractor, followed by A.

misconceptions: Equating 'least accurate' with smallest percentage uncertainty; accuracy is closeness to the accepted value
2.mcq_distractor: B - candidates picked the value with the least percentage uncertainty.

3.mcq_distractor: C - that point is under maximum tension, not compression.

misconceptions: Thinking the area under a force-time graph is work done; it is impulse/change of momentum (work done needs force-distance)

common_errors: Calculated the work done by only one force of the couple
Calculated the torque of the couple instead of the work done
good_practice: Work done by a couple = 2 x force x distance moved by each force
5.mcq_distractor: A and C were most popular; C is the work done by one force only, and B came from calculating torque.

common_errors: Mistook an LED symbol for an LDR
6.mcq_distractor: A - the LED in circuit A was confused with an LDR.

common_errors: Omitted the 2000 hours (option A)
Used only 12 W (B) or only 60 W (D) instead of the difference in power
Ignored the statement that the volume stays constant
misconceptions: Thinking only length changes when a wire is stretched; area decreases by the same factor so R scales with the square of the length factor
9.mcq_distractor: C - simply 1.50 times the original resistance.

good_practice: Wrote sin C = 1/n and saw that the largest n gives the smallest critical angle

misconceptions: Not combining P = Fv with F proportional to v^2 to get P proportional to v^3
good_practice: Wrote the key equation and proportionality, then went straight to the answer
13.mcq_distractor: All distractors were roughly equally popular; under a quarter scored.

common_errors: Used the wrong displacement (e.g. 12.7 cm) instead of 0.102 m
good_practice: Used s = 1/2 at^2 with the correct distance

common_errors: Wrote momentum instead of moment
Stated that no external forces act
Stated that the object travels at constant speed
misconceptions: Confusing the conditions for equilibrium with having no forces or constant speed
good_practice: Resultant moment is zero (principle of moments)

common_errors: Named the ball or the table as experiencing the pair force to the weight
misconceptions: Not recognising that the third-law partner of the weight acts on the Earth
Treating weight and normal contact force as a Newton's third law pair
good_practice: Stated third-law pairs are the same type of force and act on different objects; W is gravitational and N is electrostatic

common_errors: Only one vertical component correct
good_practice: Resolved both tensions vertically using the correct angles
Alternative: triangle of forces with cosine rule

common_errors: Used g = 10 m s^-2 instead of 9.81
Gave the ratio as 1.29 or 0.78
good_practice: Used x = FL/(EA) so x is proportional to F/E; both increase by 1.29 so ratio is 1.00

common_errors: Contradictory statements such as slowing down because accelerating upwards
misconceptions: Ball reaches terminal velocity before impact
Ball accelerates again after the bounce
good_practice: Stated gradient of s-t graph equals velocity and used acceleration/deceleration correctly; rebound speed lower than impact speed
v = u + at with u = 0 giving 4.905 m/s

common_errors: Drew the tangent at a time other than t = 0.50 s
Subtracted speeds (4.9 - 3.5) instead of adding because the direction reverses
Used force = weight of the ball
Used 0.50 s instead of 1.8 ms
Used only one of the velocities
misconceptions: Ignoring the vector nature of velocity/momentum on rebound

common_errors: Premature rounding
Combined all three resistances in parallel or all in series

good_practice: Used total power = e.m.f. x current (1.4 x 0.76)
